sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the Torah begins with the laws of a Hebrew slave because the perfection of servitude is with delight and vitality, which is specifically found in the Hebrew slave, and details the three levels of servants corresponding to the wicked, the intermediate, and the righteous.

translations.translation: Based on this, it will be understood why the beginning of the portion is with the law of a Hebrew slave,
even though the main subject of servitude is with a Canaanite slave
(as above, section 2),
because the perfection of the matter of servitude
(acceptance of the yoke)
is that the nullification of servitude should be with delight and vitality,
and this matter is specifically with a Hebrew slave.
This will be understood based on what the Alter Rebbe said in the discourse "And when a man sells his daughter as a maidservant"56
[and the Tzemach Tzedek writes57
about this discourse that it is a very precious discourse that speaks about the matter of the righteous, the wicked, and the intermediate],
that the three types of slaves in the portion of Mishpatim,
the Canaanite slave, the Hebrew slave, and the Hebrew maidservant,
are three levels in the service of G-d.
The Canaanite slave is one whose will and delight are in throwing off the yoke,
as our sages said,58
"A slave prefers to be ownerless,"
that his pleasure
(preference)
is in ownerlessness,
throwing off the yoke,
and his service of G-d is only out of compulsion,
due to fear of the striking of the rod,
the matter of the striking of the rod in spirituality being that his G-dly soul shines within him
(except that the revelation of the G-dly soul is only regarding actual deed).
[And it is explained there,59
that in the slave
(Canaanite)
is also included the wicked who has good.
For just as with a literal slave,
it is possible that the slave will sin against his master and nevertheless when his master strikes him with a rod he returns to his service,
so too in the service of G-d,
even one who, because his delight is in throwing off the yoke, transgresses the commandments of G-d,
nevertheless,
since afterwards,
when the revelation of his G-dly soul shines within him
(the striking of the rod)
he regrets his sins,
he does not leave the category of slave.
And on the other hand,
even the intermediate
(the lower level of the intermediate)
is included in the Canaanite slave.
For although he never committed a transgression in his life,60
nevertheless,
since his will and delight are in the desires of this world and his service of G-d is only out of compulsion
(except that the revelation of the G-dly soul compels him to turn from evil and do good throughout the entire day),
he does not leave the category of Canaanite slave].
And the Hebrew slave is one whose will and delight are
(primarily)
in the service of G-d,
and matters of throwing off the yoke
(including delight in worldly matters)
are for him great suffering and pain.61
And although when worldly matters come to him he takes delight in them,
his will is not to be drawn after them.
And he is embittered that he took delight in worldly matters.
[And this is the main level of the intermediate].
And the Hebrew maidservant is the level of the righteous,
whose attributes have been transformed to holiness
(transformation, which is above suppression),
as explained there at length.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the portion of Mishpatim primarily discusses the acquisition of the Hebrew slave and maidservant because the service of G-d must be with delight, and the Canaanite slave is mentioned only incidentally, due to the advantage of suppression.

translations.translation: And this is why in the portion of Mishpatim it speaks about the acquisition of a Hebrew slave and a Hebrew maidservant
[“When you acquire a Hebrew slave…” and “When a man sells his daughter as a maidservant”62
etc.],
and the matter of the Canaanite slave
(in the passages that speak about acquisitions of a slave63),
“She shall not go out as the slaves go out,”62
is only in an incidental manner
(and in a negative way),
because the fact that the beginning of the portion of Mishpatim is with the laws of a slave is because in this portion
[which is a continuation of the Giving of the Torah,
“Just as the first ones were from Sinai, so too these are from Sinai”]
it speaks about the general matter of the service of G-d,
which must be in the manner of the service of a slave,
and since servitude must be with delight and vitality,
therefore it speaks about the laws of a Hebrew slave and a Hebrew maidservant.
First it speaks about the Hebrew slave,
the level of the intermediate,
because the trait of the intermediate is the trait of every person, and “after the majority of people one inclines.”64
And afterwards it speaks about the Hebrew maidservant,
the level of the righteous,
for this service is also relevant to everyone,
as explained in Tanya,65
that even when one knows in his soul that he will not truly reach this level, nevertheless he does his part to fulfill the oath administered to him, “Be righteous.”
And it can be said that the fact that it speaks
[at least incidentally]
also about the Canaanite slave,
is because of the advantage of suppression.
And as the Alter Rebbe said in the aforementioned discourse,66
that even in a completely righteous person there must be the service of a Canaanite slave,
because of the advantage inherent in suppression.
For this is what our sages said,67
“A person should not say, ‘I do not desire…’ but rather, ‘I desire, but what can I do, for my Father in heaven has decreed upon me,’”
for this need to say “I desire…” is in order that he should have the service of suppression.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that even in the service of suppression, where one arouses desire in order to act against it, this very act of suppression becomes the delight of the righteous.

translations.translation: And 4)
To note,
that in this suppression there is only the advantage of suppression.
For although in saying “I desire” he is very far from G-dliness,68
nevertheless, this saying of “I desire” is because of the commandment of the Torah,
and his intention in saying “I desire” and arousing a desire for this69
is in order that he should have the service of suppression
(that he should act against his will).
Based on this it is understood,
that the fact that the service of the righteous is not out of compulsion but rather this is their delight,
applies also regarding their service of suppression.
For although it is truly suppression,
because when they say “I desire” they are arousing their will for this,
but they force themselves and act against their will,
this very thing is their delight,
since the intention in their desire is in order that they should act against their will.
